title: ArborTech - Bulk sideload, offline licensing & runtime perf sync
summary: This was a technical deep-dive focused on delivering Redwood artifacts to ArborTech's air-gapped sites and aligning on offline licensing and GPU driver packaging. We discussed options for bulk sideloads via OCI tarball vs. encrypted rsync bundle, signed driver binaries, and the offline license token handshake. On the performance side we walked through KV cache warmup, continuous batching tradeoffs, and quantization options (4-bit vs int8) tied to expected latency/throughput targets. Action items: Redwood to send packaging checklist, sha256 manifests, and a small benchmark matrix; ArborTech to confirm driver signing requirements and internal OCP for sandbox staging.
topics: runtime optimizations: KV cache, batching, quantization
next_steps: Redwood: send offline packaging checklist and example OCI tarball manifest by 2025-11-21
ArborTech: confirm HSM/KMS constraints and driver signing policy by 2025-11-24
Schedule 2-hr pilot kickoff with ArborTech infra team week of 2025-11-25
action_items: Priya Nair | Send offline packaging checklist, sha256 manifests, and small sample tarball URL | 2025-11-21
Ethan Cole | Produce a 3-scenario benchmark matrix (kv-cache cold/warm, batching levels, quantization presets) and upload CSV | 2025-11-22
Jin Park | Share internal driver-signing requirement doc and permitted signer CNs | 2025-11-24
Nina Patel | Confirm whether HSM-backed license tokens required, and provide contact for compliance | 2025-11-24
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-19
Start: 14:00 PST
Duration: 85 minutes
Attendees: Priya Nair (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), María Santos (Redwood), Liam O'Connor (CTO, ArborTech), Jin Park (Infra Lead), Sofia Morales (ML Eng), Nina Patel (Security)

Summary / Notes (auto): discussed artifact delivery options for air-gapped sites, offline license token procedures, GPU driver packaging, and runtime perf tuning (KV cache, batching, quantization).

Transcript:
[00:00:03] Priya Nair: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll kick off — quick intros? I'll hand over to Ethan to run the technical bits.
[00:00:12] Ethan Cole: Thanks Priya. Hi Liam, Jin, Sofia, Nina. Quick agenda: artifact delivery options, offline licensing flow, GPU driver packaging, and then runtime perf — kv cache, batching, quantization and pilot plan.
[00:00:28] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. We're trying to get this into our controlled data-centers where there's no outbound internet, so the artifact side is priority.
[00:00:36] Jin Park: Also drivers — we have both older A100 nodes and some upcoming L40s in different racks. We need to know exact driver versions and whether Redwood provides signed binaries.
[00:00:47] Ethan Cole: Totally. We have two main artifact delivery patterns we've used: 1) OCI tarball exported from a disconnected registry (we generate an export .tar.gz + sha256 manifest), or 2) encrypted rsync bundle with metadata and a detached signature. For air-gapped installs the tarball is cleaner, less error-prone.
[00:01:05] Sofia Morales: Is the tarball a docker save style image or does it include the runtime lib and vendor drivers?
[00:01:11] Ethan Cole: It contains the Redwood runtime container images, pre-pulled dependencies, and optionally a driver bundle (signed) if you choose side-load drivers. Drivers are separate because of licensing — we give a signed wrapper script and fingerprints; actual NVIDIA driver blobs may be provided under a separate transfer agreement depending on region.
[00:01:29] Nina Patel: On the security side we need SHA256 checksums, signature metadata, and verified signer CNs. Our policy mandates HSM-signed artifacts for any third-party binaries. Can Redwood support that?
[00:01:39] María Santos: We can produce artifacts signed with our CI key; for HSM we can produce an intermediary signing manifest and work with your infosec to trust the key or we can coordinate a transfer of the signing key to your HSM under a signing ceremony. This is somewhat manual but we've done it for two customers.
[00:01:57] Liam O'Connor: Okay that's promising. On licensing: offline license tokens — how does that handshake work if the deployment has zero egress?
[00:02:04] Ethan Cole: Good question. Two patterns: 1) time-limited opaque license tokens we issue as files you upload into the private control plane; or 2) an offline activation where we generate a signed license bundle tied to your cluster-id and HSM public key, with a validity period. The latter is what we recommend for long-lived air-gapped deployments.
[00:02:22] Jin Park: The cluster-id — is that something we generate locally or does Redwood create it? We need to ensure it does not leak environment info.
[00:02:28] Priya Nair: The cluster-id is generated locally by a small CLI that runs entirely offline and returns a blob you send to Redwood. That blob contains only the cluster public key and a random UUID; it doesn't include inventory.
[00:02:37] Jin Park: Great. We prefer the signed license bundle approach.
[00:02:42] Ethan Cole: We'll include a sample CLI and the steps in the packaging checklist.
[00:02:48] [00:02:50] Sofia Morales: Switching to runtime perf — our SLO is 95th percentile latency < 180ms for short chat responses and sustained throughput of ~450 tokens/s per A100 for batch workloads. What tuning knobs do we need?
[00:02:59] Ethan Cole: Two axes: latency-sensitive routing and throughput-optimized batching. For low-latency we recommend small batch sizes and KV prefix caching warmed for common prompts. For throughput you enable larger batch windows, increase max_batch_size, and use continuous batching with sharding across GPUs.
[00:03:14] Ethan Cole: Also, quantization will reduce memory footprint and increase throughput — 4-bit recipes we've validated for many transformer variants, but some accuracy loss may occur. Int8 is a good middle ground for less quality drift.
[00:03:27] Sofia Morales: Have you seen deterministic regressions with 4-bit quant? We can't afford hallucination spikes for production.
[00:03:32] María Santos: We run model-specific eval suites. For OP models we've seen a 0.5-1.5% drop on our standard entailment eval with 4-bit, but for chat and instruction-following it's more complicated. We recommend canarying quantized models behind A/B rollouts and metric-based guardrails.
[00:03:48] Jin Park: On KV cache — how long does the cache warm typically take? We have a mix of workloads where prefixes vary a lot.
[00:03:55] Ethan Cole: Warmup depends on prefix overlap. For high prefix reuse, a passive prefix cache (sync on read) warms under tens of seconds. For broader variance we use precomputed prefix checkpoints for common prompt templates — that's part of Redwood Optimize. Precompute shipping of KV snapshots can be included in the artifact bundle.
[00:04:13] Priya Nair: Quick clarification — when you say precomputed checkpoints, that's an optional artifact we can generate from your on-prem prompt set, correct?
[00:04:19] María Santos: Correct. You upload a representative prompt corpus in the staging phase, we produce KV snapshots tuned to the model and sequence lengths, and that becomes part of the sideload bundle.
[00:04:26] Nina Patel: About telemetry — because we are air-gapped we can't send token-level metrics back. What observability can run locally and how do we reconcile with Redwood console?
[00:04:34] Ethan Cole: For private deployments we provide a local observability stack that writes to a local time-series store. We can produce periodic whitebox diagnostic bundles that you can share via secure transfer. For the hosted console features you get a stripped-down offline CSV export that can be manually uploaded.
[00:04:47] Jin Park: Driver specifics: do you require NVIDIA driver 525+ for L40 features and what about CUDA toolkits?
[00:04:52] Ethan Cole: For A100 we typically target driver 515+ with CUDA 11.8; for L40 we recommend 525+ with CUDA 12.x. We'll provide per-image driver compatibility notes. Also if you plan to use NCCL all-reduce across racks in a restricted network, we support NCCL 2.14+ and require certain multicast/UC settings — we'll put the exact kernel modules in the checklist.
[00:05:10] Sofia Morales: Are there any known perf cliffs if a driver mismatch happens? Like will the runtime degrade silently or error out?
[00:05:16] María Santos: Minor mismatches will usually fail to load optimized kernels and fall back to slower generic kernels — you'll see higher latency and higher GPU memory use. In worst case, some kernels can fail at runtime producing errors. That's why we recommend a preflight script included in the bundle that validates driver/version/kernel ABI and reports an offline-friendly report.
[00:05:33] Liam O'Connor: What's in that preflight report?
[00:05:36] Ethan Cole: Kernel modules, driver version, available GPU memory, nvml results, and a small synthetic throughput/latency test (single token and 32-token batch) that outputs CSV + sha256 for audit.
[00:05:47] [00:05:48] Jin Park: On packaging — do you support both RPM and DEB repos for the side-loaded packages?
[00:05:53] Priya Nair: Yes; we can provide both and also a containerized runtime image as the primary mechanism. For systems that can't run our container runtime we provide an unpacked artifact set and systemd service definitions.
[00:06:03] Nina Patel: We need reproducible builds. How do you ensure the tarball isn't modified after signing?
[00:06:08] María Santos: We provide a signed manifest including file-level sha256 and a top-level signature. The preflight checks verify manifest vs files. For HSM integration we can produce a chain-of-trust doc.
[00:06:18] Sofia Morales: Back to KV cache and batching — do you have adaptive batching? Like variable time slices based on latency SLO?
[00:06:24] Ethan Cole: Yes, runtime supports adaptive batching policy: you set latency SLOs and a policy that shrinks batch window dynamically under load to meet p95 goals; when idle it expands for throughput. We also support priority routing for token-critical requests that skip batching.
[00:06:37] Sofia Morales: Any rough numbers for CPU/GPU memory overhead for larger batch sizes? Our nodes have 80GB per GPU.
[00:06:43] María Santos: It depends on model and KV cache. For a 30B param model quantized to 4-bit you might see model footprint ~12–18GB, KV cache scales with context length and batch concurrency — we provide a sizing spreadsheet. For 32-token batches, plan for additional ~6–8GB of temporary allocation per GPU. We'll share a worked example.
[00:07:01] Ethan Cole: Also note continuous batching with multi-GPU sharding reduces per-GPU overhead but increases interconnect traffic — so if your racks have 100GbE vs NVLink that changes optimal config.
[00:07:13] Jin Park: We have NVLink across pairs and 100GbE within racks. So sharding inside rack is fine, cross-rack we prefer RPC.
[00:07:19] Ethan Cole: Perfect — we'll recommend shard-by-rack config.
[00:07:23] [00:07:25] Sofia Morales: On quantization: is the pipeline for quantizing models included in the artifact or do you ship pre-quantized model files?
[00:07:31] María Santos: We can do either. Pre-quantized models are simpler for offline installs; if you want to run your own quantization pipeline we provide the tooling and config, but that requires building in a CUDA-enabled environment. For air-gapped we usually include pre-quantized model files plus the recipe and a checksum.
[00:07:46] Nina Patel: Will pre-quantized models be deterministic across runs? We need reproducible outputs for compliance.
[00:07:51] Ethan Cole: There is some non-determinism with mixed precision ops and certain GPU kernels, but we offer a deterministic mode that pins algorithm choices at a modest perf cost. We'll call out what that cost looks like in the benchmark matrix.
[00:08:03] Liam O'Connor: Okay, sounds like a clear path. Next — pilot scope. We want to validate: 1) artifact install in staging air-gapped host, 2) driver validation, 3) 3 perf tests: cold kv, warm kv, and high-concurrency batching.
[00:08:16] Priya Nair: Proposed pilot schedule: day 0 transfer tarball and manifest; day 1 preflight and driver install; day 2 run predefined perf suite; day 3 review and remediate. Does that align?
[00:08:24] Jin Park: Yes. We'll need a dry-run on an isolated VM first.
[00:08:28] Ethan Cole: We'll provide step-by-step runbook and the synthetic test harness. We'll also provide the benchmark CSV so you can replicate.
[00:08:35] [00:08:36] Sofia Morales: A couple of nitty-gritty questions: how big is the tarball typically? We have limited offline transfer windows — 16GB usb transfers are common.
[00:08:43] María Santos: Typical full bundle with models is big — 200–400GB. For pilot we create a minisample build with trimmed model (sliced seq length and smaller model) that's under 12–16GB. Full production bundles are shipped on encrypted drives or via secure courier.
[00:08:58] Jin Park: We prefer the encrypted drive route for the production sync. For pilot the sample tarball is fine.
[00:09:03] Priya Nair: We'll prepare a minisample bundle for the pilot and include the preflight and the sample driver package.
[00:09:09] [00:09:11] Nina Patel: From compliance, we also need a retention plan for logs and a truncated telemetry option. Can Redwood support local-only retention windows and scrub PII before any bundle export?
[00:09:19] Ethan Cole: Yes, local-only retention is standard for Private deployments. We can include a scrubber script that anonymizes user tokens. That will be part of the deployment options in the runbook.
[00:09:28] Liam O'Connor: Any blockers we're seeing that would prevent us moving to the reserved capacity or Dedicated offering?
[00:09:34] Priya Nair: Not from a technical standpoint — mostly commercial and timeline. Once pilot is green we'll share Dedicated sizing and committed capacity options.
[00:09:41] [00:09:43] Sofia Morales: One more technical: if we need to roll back to a previous model version quickly in air-gapped, how are rollbacks handled without access to the registry?
[00:09:50] María Santos: We advise keeping a two-tier artifact snapshot strategy: active and rollback bundles. Each bundle is checksumed and versioned. Our control plane (private/offline) supports toggling route config locally to point to the rollback artifact. We'll include instructions.
[00:10:03] Ethan Cole: Okay — time check, we have about 75 minutes left for deeper discussion and questions, but maybe we should move to specific next steps so folks can action.
[00:10:12] Liam O'Connor: Agreed. Could you confirm the exact artifacts you'll send?
[00:10:15] Priya Nair: We'll send: 1) offline packaging checklist and preflight script; 2) minisample tarball manifest (sha256) and download instructions; 3) driver sample and signing manifest; 4) benchmark matrix CSV; 5) runbook for pilot.
[00:10:27] Jin Park: And the CLI for generating cluster-id and an example license bundle?
[00:10:30] Ethan Cole: Yes, sample CLI + example signed license bundle for staging.
[00:10:34] Nina Patel: Can you also include the signer CNs and the public key fingerprint in the manifest?
[00:10:38] María Santos: We'll include a signer table and sample PGP/HSM fingerprint entries.
[00:10:42] [00:10:44] Priya Nair: Great. Do we want to lock a pilot kickoff date now?
[00:10:47] Jin Park: Week of 2025-11-25 is best for us. We'll confirm after internal calendar check.
[00:10:53] Priya Nair: Perfect. We'll email the artifacts and propose two time slots for the kickoff.
[00:10:58] [00:11:00] Sofia Morales: Quick follow-up on NCCL — if cross-rack all-reduce is disabled we still support model-parallel in the runtime?
[00:11:06] María Santos: We support tensor and pipeline parallelism with fallback RPC for cross-rack. Performance will be reduced compared to NVLink but it's supported. We'll document expected throughput deltas.
[00:11:16] Liam O'Connor: Okay everyone, thanks — this was useful. Any last-minute points?
[00:11:21] Jin Park: None from infra. We'll look for the manifest and the preflight script.
[00:11:25] Nina Patel: We'll follow up on HSM signing details with Redwood security.
[00:11:29] Priya Nair: Thanks all — we'll send materials by 11/21 and follow up on the pilot slot.
[00:11:36] [END OF MAIN CONVERSATION]

Post-meeting notes (auto):
- Redwood will prepare minisample tarball ~12–16GB for pilot and full encrypted drive options for production shipments.
- Attachments to be sent: packaging checklist, preflight, sample driver, benchmark CSV, runbook, sample license bundle.
- Redwood SE to produce benchmark scenarios including cold KV, warm KV, and batch scaling profiles.

Transcript quality notes: audio was clear but occasional microphone overlap; some product names were auto-corrected by transcription (e.g., NVLink transcribed as 'N link' in places).
